chatbot_metadata.description: A comprehensive chatbot knowledge base for gastritis, gastroparesis, and digestive health, compiled from medical documents and dietary guides.
sources: New Approaches in Gastritis Treatment (InTech, Marcial et al., 2011)
NIDDK (National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases) – Gastritis & Gastropathy (2025)
ACG Clinical Practice Guideline: H. pylori Treatment 2024
Mayo Clinic – IBS Symptoms, Causes & Diagnosis (2024)

gastritis.definition: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining (gastric mucosa). The mucosal barrier normally protects the stomach from acid and pepsin; gastritis occurs when this balance is disrupted, allowing irritation and inflammation.

types.name: Acute Gastritis
types.description: Sudden inflammation of the stomach lining, ranging from mild to severe. Classic symptoms are nausea and pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen.

types.name: Chronic Gastritis
types.description: Progressive inflammation developing gradually over time; often initially asymptomatic. Symptoms may include dull upper abdominal pain, fullness, and loss of appetite.

types.name: Reactive/Chemical Gastritis
types.description: Defined by foveolar elongation, edema, and vasodilatation with few inflammatory cells. Results from duodenogastric bile reflux or NSAIDs use.

types.name: Acute Stress Gastritis
types.description: Most serious form; occurs in critically ill patients (e.g., ICU). Stress erosions may develop suddenly as a result of severe trauma.

types.name: Atrophic Gastritis
types.description: Results from chronic gastritis leading to atrophy (wasting away) of the gastric lining. Final stage of chronic gastritis; may be a precursor to gastric cancer.

types.name: Hemorrhagic Gastritis
types.description: Caused by superficial erosions leading to bleeding.

types.name: Eosinophilic Gastritis
types.description: Rare type characterized by eosinophils in the mucosa, sometimes linked to food allergies.

types.name: Lymphocytic Gastritis
types.description: Chronic inflammation characterized by lymphocyte accumulation in the gastric mucosa.

symptoms: Stomach pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen
Note: Some people with chronic gastritis may have NO symptoms
diagnosis: Endoscopy or gastroscopy to examine the stomach lining
Biopsy to detect H. pylori and assess tissue changes
H. pylori breath test or stool antigen test
X-rays or barium swallow to identify structural abnormalities

key_causes.NSAID_damage: NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen) cause gastric damage by: (1) direct topical irritation on the gastric epithelium; (2) systemic suppression of mucosal prostaglandin synthesis. This reduces mucus/bicarbonate secretion, blood flow, cell turnover, and repair.
key_causes.H_pylori: H. pylori is the most aggressive cause of gastritis. The bacteria uses adhesins on its outer cell wall to attach to gastric mucus and epithelial cells, establishing infection. Untreated infection can lead to gastric ulcer or gastric cancer.
key_causes.dietary_factors: Acidic foods (citrus, tomatoes), carbonated drinks, coffee, alcohol, excessively hot/cold foods, processed foods, excessive salt, and overeating all contribute to gastric irritation.
key_causes.stress: Chronic stress decreases protective gastric factors, increases acid production, and may lead to unhealthy coping behaviors (alcohol, smoking, poor diet).
key_causes.other: Imbalanced diet, abrasive compounds, stomach acid damaging its own lining

key_facts: The majority of people with gastritis or gastropathy do NOT have any symptoms.
H. pylori gastritis is one of the most common types — it is chronic and a major cause of peptic ulcer disease.
H. pylori may spread through contact with an infected person's vomit, stool, or saliva, or through contaminated food or water.
Autoimmune gastritis can cause problems absorbing iron and vitamin B12 from food.
Less common causes include infections with viruses, parasites, fungi, and bacteria other than H. pylori, typically in people with weakened immune systems.
Gastritis may lead to erosions or ulcers, causing stomach bleeding — symptoms include black/tarry stool or red/maroon blood in stool (seek emergency care immediately).
Researchers have not found that eating, diet, and nutrition play a major role in causing most cases of gastritis or gastropathy.

procedures: Upper GI Endoscopy with biopsy — doctor uses a flexible tube with a camera (endoscope) to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum; biopsies taken to detect H. pylori and tissue changes.
Upper GI Series (Barium swallow) — X-ray procedure using barium to check for signs of gastritis or gastropathy.
H. pylori urea breath test — patient swallows a liquid containing urea; if H. pylori present, it breaks it down into carbon dioxide detectable in breath.
H. pylori stool antigen test — detects H. pylori antigens in stool sample.
Blood tests — for anemia, autoimmune antibodies, vitamin B12 levels.
when_to_seek_emergency_care: Red or maroon blood in stool

gastroparesis.definition: Gastroparesis (also called delayed gastric emptying) is a disorder in which the stomach takes too long to empty its contents into the small intestine. It happens when the nerves to the stomach are damaged or stop working.
symptoms: Feeling full quickly when eating (early satiety)
Erratic blood sugar levels (especially in diabetics)
gastroparesis.diabetes_connection: Diabetes increases the risk for gastroparesis. Gastroparesis causes unpredictable food absorption, leading to erratic blood sugar levels. High blood sugar directly interferes with normal stomach emptying. Managing blood sugar is a key part of managing diabetic gastroparesis.

official_source_niddk.definition_expanded: Gastroparesis is a disorder that slows or stops the movement of food from your stomach to your small intestine, even though there is no blockage. The condition lasts at least 3 months in the absence of mechanical obstruction. It involves abnormalities in gastrointestinal motor function, including the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems, gastric smooth muscle cells, pacemaker cells, and the pyloric sphincter.
official_source_niddk.epidemiology: Incidence ranges from 6.3 to 17.2 per 100,000 person-years. Nausea is the most common symptom, reported in over 90% of patients. Vomiting and bloating affect 68–84% and 75% of patients respectively.

causes_by_prevalence.notes: Cannot be prevented; no identifiable cause
Most common known cause; high blood glucose directly worsens stomach emptying
Hypothyroidism, Parkinson's disease, scleroderma, certain medications

diagnosis: Gastric emptying scintigraphy (GES) — nuclear medicine test, gold standard; measures how fast food leaves the stomach
Gastric emptying breath test (GEBT) — non-radioactive alternative
Upper endoscopy — to rule out blockage or other diseases
Upper GI series — X-ray with barium
Gastric manometry — measures pressure and movement in stomach muscles
complications: Bezoar formation (hardened mass of undigested food that can block stomach emptying)
Erratic blood glucose levels (especially dangerous in diabetes)

dietary_management: Eat 6 small meals per day instead of 3 large ones
Start with liquids when symptoms are severe; advance to soft/pureed foods as tolerated
Reduce fat intake — fat slows gastric emptying
Reduce fiber intake — high fiber can cause bezoar formation
Chew all food to mashed potato/pudding consistency
Sit upright for at least 1 hour after eating
Drink fluids between meals, not during
Keep blood glucose within target range if diabetic — hyperglycemia worsens gastroparesis

medications.name: Metoclopramide
medications.notes: Only FDA-approved drug for gastroparesis in the US. Helps stomach muscles work better. Maximum 12 weeks use due to risk of tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements).

medications.name: Domperidone
medications.notes: Available in some countries; not FDA-approved in the US. Can cause cardiac side effects.

medications.name: Erythromycin
medications.notes: Low-dose erythromycin improves gastric emptying through motilin receptor stimulation. Short-term use preferred.

medications.name: Antiemetics (Prochlorperazine, Diphenhydramine, Ondansetron)
medications.notes: Provide symptomatic relief of nausea and vomiting. Do not improve gastric emptying.

medications.name: Non-narcotic pain medicines
medications.notes: For abdominal pain due to gastroparesis; narcotic opioids should be avoided as they worsen gastroparesis.

surgical_and_procedural.name: Gastric Electrical Stimulation (GES)
surgical_and_procedural.description: A device surgically implanted in the abdomen that sends mild electrical pulses to the stomach muscles. Used only for diabetes-related or idiopathic gastroparesis when medications fail. Not suitable for all patients.

surgical_and_procedural.name: Jejunostomy tube (J-tube)
surgical_and_procedural.description: Feeding tube placed directly into the small intestine to bypass the stomach entirely — used in severe malnutrition cases.

surgical_and_procedural.name: Parenteral nutrition
surgical_and_procedural.description: IV nutrition delivered directly into the bloodstream — for the most severe cases.

surgical_and_procedural.name: Botulinum toxin injection (pylorus)
surgical_and_procedural.description: Injection into the pyloric sphincter to relax it and improve emptying. Evidence is limited.

IBS_and_bloating.definition: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and associated gas/bloating can be triggered by fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) that pull excess water into the small intestine and are fermented by gut bacteria, producing gas.
IBS_and_bloating.FODMAP_explanation: FODMAP stands for Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, And Polyols. These are poorly absorbed carbohydrates and sugar alcohols found in many foods. They draw excess water into the small intestine and are fermented by gut bacteria, causing bloating, gas, pain, and altered bowel habits.

official_source_mayo.prevalence: Affects approximately 7–16% of the US population; about 1 in 10 adults. Most common in women and people under 50.

ibs_types.description: Mostly constipation, hard or lumpy stools
Mostly diarrhea, loose or watery stools
Doesn't fit cleanly into above categories

official_source_mayo.rome_iv_diagnostic_criteria: Recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day per week on average, associated with 2+ of: (1) related to defecation, (2) associated with change in stool frequency, (3) associated with change in stool form/appearance.
causes_and_mechanisms: Disorder of gut-brain interaction — bidirectional communication between brain and gut is dysregulated
Visceral hypersensitivity — gut nerves more sensitive than normal
Psychological stress amplifies symptoms through gut-brain axis
Post-infectious IBS can develop after a GI infection
Hormonal factors — more common and worse symptoms in women
alarm_symptoms_requiring_medical_evaluat: Symptoms occurring at night during normal sleeping hours
Abdominal pain unrelieved by bowel movement

lifestyle: Deep breathing and yoga to reduce stress
Identify and avoid personal food triggers
Maintain a consistent daily eating schedule
dietary: Low FODMAP diet — most evidence-based dietary approach for IBS
Increase soluble fiber gradually (e.g., psyllium/ispaghula husk)
Avoid known trigger foods (varies per individual)
Limit caffeine, alcohol, fatty foods, and carbonated drinks

medications.name: Low-dose antidepressants (TCAs, SSRIs)
medications.use: Gut-brain axis modulation; particularly for pain

medications.name: Rifaximin (antibiotic)
medications.use: IBS-D — targets gut bacteria causing symptoms

medications.name: Peppermint oil capsules
medications.use: Antispasmodic effect on gut muscles; reduces pain

psychological_therapies: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — strong evidence for IBS
treatment_overview.important_note: There is currently no cure for IBS. IBS does NOT cause permanent damage to the intestines and does NOT increase cancer risk. Symptoms can be well-managed with the right combination of diet, lifestyle, and medication.

GERD.definition: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) occurs when stomach acid frequently flows back (refluxes) into the esophagus, irritating the lining. It is a chronic, often lifelong condition.
GERD.prevalence: Affects approximately 20% of adults in Western countries. One of the most common gastrointestinal conditions worldwide.
symptoms: Heartburn — burning sensation in chest, usually after eating, worse when lying down
Acid regurgitation — sour or bitter taste in mouth
Feeling of a lump in the throat
Chronic cough, laryngitis, or new/worsening asthma (atypical symptoms)
causes_and_risk_factors: Weakened or abnormally relaxed lower esophageal sphincter (LES)
Certain foods and beverages (fatty foods, chocolate, mint, alcohol, coffee, acidic foods)
Certain medications (aspirin, ibuprofen, calcium channel blockers)
complications: Barrett's esophagus (pre-cancerous cell change in esophagus lining)
Esophageal cancer (rare, associated with Barrett's esophagus)
diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on symptoms (most common)
Upper GI endoscopy — to assess esophageal damage
Ambulatory acid (pH) probe test — measures acid in esophagus over 24 hours

lifestyle_changes: Do not lie down within 2-3 hours of eating
Elevate head of bed by 6-8 inches
Avoid trigger foods (chocolate, mint, fatty foods, acidic foods, caffeine, alcohol)

medications.name: Antacids (Tums, Rolaids, Maalox)
medications.use: Quick symptom relief; neutralize acid; do not heal esophagus

medications.name: H2 receptor blockers (Famotidine)
medications.use: Reduce acid production; faster onset than PPIs

medications.name: Proton Pump Inhibitors / PPIs (Omeprazole, Esomeprazole, Lansoprazole)
medications.use: Most effective for reducing acid production and healing esophagus; first-line for moderate-severe GERD

medications.name: Prokinetics (Metoclopramide)
medications.use: Helps stomach empty faster; used if delayed gastric emptying is contributing

medications.name: Baclofen
medications.use: Reduces frequency of LES relaxations; used in refractory GERD

treatment.surgery: Fundoplication (Nissen fundoplication) — surgical procedure wrapping stomach top around LES to strengthen it. Considered when lifestyle + medications fail or patient prefers to avoid long-term medication.

foods_that_help: Non-acidic vegetables (green beans, broccoli, asparagus, cauliflower, leafy greens)
Whole grains (oatmeal, brown rice, whole grain bread)

peptic_ulcer.definition: Peptic ulcers are open sores that develop on the inner lining of the stomach (gastric ulcer), the upper portion of the small intestine (duodenal ulcer), or rarely the esophagus. They occur when the protective mucus layer is reduced or stomach acid erodes the lining.
symptoms: Burning stomach pain (most common) — may improve with eating or antacids
Feeling of fullness, bloating, or belching
Dark, tarry, or bloody stools (severe — seek emergency care)

causes.notes: Most common cause globally; bacteria weaken mucus protective coating
Block prostaglandin synthesis that protects stomach lining; especially risky with long-term use
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (rare) causes overproduction of stomach acid
Increases stomach acid and reduces healing

treatment.h_pylori_related: H. pylori eradication therapy (see H. pylori treatment 2024 section) + PPI for mucosal healing
treatment.nsaid_related: Stop or reduce NSAIDs; use PPIs or misoprostol for gastroprotection; consider acetaminophen as alternative
general: PPIs for 4-8 weeks to heal the ulcer
Avoid smoking and alcohol during healing
diet_guidance: Avoid spicy foods, acidic foods, coffee, and alcohol
Probiotics may help restore gut flora during antibiotic therapy
Cabbage juice has traditional use for ulcers (contains glutamine)
Honey (especially Manuka honey) shows mild H. pylori inhibitory effects in some studies

when_to_see_doctor_urgently: Vomiting blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Blood in stool or black/tarry stool
Sudden, severe abdominal pain (possible perforation — emergency)

gastritis_drugs.mechanism: Block the proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase), suppressing gastric acid secretion by over 80% at 40mg dose.
gastritis_drugs.use: First-line treatment for gastritis, peptic ulcers, H. pylori eradication (as part of triple therapy), NSAID-induced gastropathy.
gastritis_drugs.notes: Side effects possible with long-term use. May contribute to gastric gland toxicity; Vitamin C co-administration may mitigate this.

gastritis_drugs.mechanism: Block histamine H2 receptors, reducing stomach acid production.
gastritis_drugs.use: Gastritis, peptic ulcers, GERD. Therapy goal: raise gastric pH above 4.5.

gastritis_drugs.mechanism: Neutralize existing stomach acid; some (sucralfate) also coat and protect the mucosal lining.
gastritis_drugs.use: Symptom relief; gastroprotection especially when co-prescribed with NSAIDs.

gastritis_drugs.mechanism: Synthetic prostaglandin E1 that protects the gastric mucosa by stimulating mucus/bicarbonate secretion and reducing acid.

gastritis_drugs.notes: Success rate approximately 80%, decreasing worldwide due to H. pylori antibiotic resistance. Side effects from multiple drugs are common.

therapy_goals: Raise gastric pH above 4.5 to stop autodigestive processes
Raise pH above 6.0 for treating actively bleeding peptic ulcers

key_changes_from_2017: Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (BQT) is now the PREFERRED first-line treatment — NOT clarithromycin-based triple therapy.
Clarithromycin and levofloxacin-based regimens are NOT recommended unless susceptibility testing confirms effectiveness.
In the US, clarithromycin, metronidazole, and levofloxacin resistance rates exceed 30%; amoxicillin, rifabutin, and tetracycline resistance remains low.
14-day treatment duration recommended for all regimens (achieves >90% eradication vs 75-85% for triple therapy).
Vonoprazan (potassium-competitive acid blocker / PCAB) is now recognized as an alternative to PPI in dual or triple therapy.

first_line_regimens.name: Optimized Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (BQT) — PREFERRED
first_line_regimens.notes: Do NOT substitute doxycycline for tetracycline (reduces eradication by 10-17%). Each drug must be at sufficient dose and frequency.

first_line_regimens.name: Rifabutin Triple Therapy
first_line_regimens.notes: Alternative first-line option for patients without penicillin allergy.

first_line_regimens.name: Vonoprazan Dual Therapy
first_line_regimens.notes: New approach using potent acid blocker. Recognized in 2024 ACG guideline.

salvage_therapy: Optimized BQT if not previously used
Rifabutin triple therapy if BQT was previously used
Susceptibility-guided therapy is ideal but testing is not always accessible
h_pylori_updated_2024.global_prevalence: H. pylori infects approximately half the world's population (systematic review, Gastroenterology 2017)
h_pylori_updated_2024.eradication_importance: Eradication is strongly linked to preventing peptic ulcer recurrence and reducing gastric cancer risk. Chronic H. pylori infection is the leading risk factor for gastric cancer.

probiotics_LAB.overview: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species are proposed as natural alternatives for gastric health. They resist acid and bile, can transiently colonize the stomach, and competitively exclude pathogenic bacteria.

key_strains.name: Lactobacillus reuteri ATCC 55730
key_strains.benefit: Colonizes the GI tract and generates immune responses; stimulates T-helper cells in the ileum.

key_strains.name: L. johnsonii La1
key_strains.benefit: Pronounced anti-inflammatory effect on H. pylori-associated gastritis; reduces pro-inflammatory chemokines in gastric mucosa.

key_strains.name: L. casei
key_strains.benefit: Inhibits H. pylori growth; reduces urease activity in gastric epithelial cells.

key_strains.name: L. acidophilus
key_strains.benefit: Bactericidal activity against H. pylori; used in probiotic fermented milk products.

key_strains.name: Bifidobacterium bifidum CECT 7366
key_strains.benefit: Partially relieves H. pylori-induced gastric tissue damage; decreases H. pylori pathogenicity.

key_strains.name: Streptococcus thermophilus CRL 1190
key_strains.benefit: EPS-producing strain shown to prevent and treat chronic gastritis in animal models; activates mucin synthesis; modulates inflammatory cytokines (reduces TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma; increases IL-10).

probiotics_LAB.exopolysaccharides: EPS (exopolysaccharides) produced by certain LAB strains can inhibit H. pylori adhesion to the mucus layer, strengthen the mucus barrier, and modulate mucosal immune responses.
probiotic_foods: Commercially available probiotic supplements (consult healthcare provider for strain selection)

medicinal_plants.overview: Plant extracts have been used for centuries for gastric conditions. Active compounds include phenolics, flavonoids, polysaccharides, terpenes, and essential oils. Always consult a healthcare provider before use.

notable_plants.name: Green Tea (Camellia sinensis)
notable_plants.benefit: Inhibits H. pylori urease; bactericidal and bacteriostatic effects in vitro; consumption before infection prevents mucosal inflammation; after infection reduces gastritis severity.

notable_plants.name: Licorice Root (Glycyrrhiza glabra)
notable_plants.active_compound: Polysaccharides (arabinose, galactose, glucose, glucuronic acid); DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice extract)
notable_plants.benefit: Interacts with H. pylori outer-membrane adhesins, preventing adhesion to gastric mucus. DGL increases gastric mucus and bicarbonate production; has bactericidal properties.
notable_plants.use: Syrup, tea, chewable tablets (DGL form preferred for long-term use)

notable_plants.name: Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla)
notable_plants.benefit: Soothing and anti-inflammatory properties; calms stomach pain.
notable_plants.use: Steep chamomile flowers in boiled water; let cool before drinking

notable_plants.name: Aloe Vera
notable_plants.benefit: Anti-inflammatory and regenerative effects on gastric mucosa.
notable_plants.use: Pure juice (1/4 to 1/2 cup) or freeze-dried powder between or before meals; remove outer layer to avoid irritants

notable_plants.name: Cranberry Juice
notable_plants.benefit: High molecular mass constituent inhibits H. pylori adhesion to human gastric mucus and erythrocytes.

notable_plants.name: Turmeric (Curcuma longa)
notable_plants.benefit: Reduces serum nitric oxide and lipid peroxidation in gastritis; inhibits iNOS expression; maintains cellular glutathione stores.

notable_plants.name: Peppermint (Mentha piperita)
notable_plants.benefit: Digestive and anti-flatulence; relieves gastritis, dyspepsia, and biliary disorders.
notable_plants.use: Infusion/tea (NOTE: avoid in GERD/reflux as it can relax the lower esophageal sphincter)

notable_plants.name: Slippery Elm
notable_plants.benefit: Soothes and protects the stomach lining.
notable_plants.use: One teaspoon of powder in warm water before meals

notable_plants.name: Pomegranate (Punica granatum)
notable_plants.benefit: Anti-ulcer activity; hepatoprotective; tonic effect on gastric diseases.

notable_plants.name: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus)
notable_plants.benefit: Inhibits adhesion of H. pylori to human gastric mucosa.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: DGL (Deglycyrrhizinated Licorice)
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Increases gastric mucus and bicarbonate production; safe for long-term use; bactericidal properties.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Slippery Elm
supplements_for_gastritis.dosage: 1 teaspoon powder in warm water before meals
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Contains mucilage that coats and protects the stomach lining.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: L-Glutamine
supplements_for_gastritis.dosage: 5–10 grams daily on an empty stomach
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Amino acid supporting cell health; repairs stomach lining; helps prevent toxins entering bloodstream.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Zinc Carnosine
supplements_for_gastritis.dosage: 150 mg per day in divided doses
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Supports gastric healing and reduces inflammation without inhibiting stomach acid.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Aloe Vera Juice
supplements_for_gastritis.dosage: 1/4 to 1/2 cup between or before meals

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Probiotics
supplements_for_gastritis.dosage: Varies by strain; consult healthcare provider
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Promotes gut health; may help manage H. pylori-associated gastritis.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Digestive Enzymes
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Aid food breakdown and nutrient absorption. Use with care to avoid irritation.

supplements_for_gastritis.name: Multivitamins
supplements_for_gastritis.benefit: Prevent deficiencies common in gastritis (especially vitamin B12 and iron). Use non-irritating forms (sprays or sublinguals).

home_remedies.name: Potato Juice
home_remedies.preparation: Juice raw potatoes and consume immediately.
home_remedies.benefit: Acts as a natural antacid; calms stomach pain.

home_remedies.name: Chamomile Tea
home_remedies.preparation: Steep chamomile flowers in boiled water; let cool before drinking.

home_remedies.name: Nopal Water (Cactus Water)
home_remedies.preparation: Soak cut nopal (prickly pear cactus) leaf in water overnight; drink before meals.
home_remedies.benefit: Gastroprotective effects due to mucilage content.

home_remedies.name: Aloe Vera Water
home_remedies.preparation: Remove the outer layer of aloe vera leaf; blend the inner gel with a little water. Consume on an empty stomach.

gastroparesis_medical.overview: Treatment of gastroparesis depends on the cause, severity, and response to therapy. Dietary modification is the first step. Medications help when diet alone is insufficient. Surgical options are reserved for severe refractory cases.

medications.name: Metoclopramide (Reglan)
medications.use: First-line FDA-approved drug for gastroparesis in the US; improves gastric motility and reduces nausea/vomiting
medications.dosage: 5-10 mg before meals and at bedtime
medications.warnings: Maximum recommended use: 12 weeks. Risk of tardive dyskinesia (involuntary muscle movements) with prolonged use — FDA black box warning.

medications.name: Erythromycin
medications.use: Low-dose erythromycin improves gastric emptying; not used for infection but for motility benefit
medications.warnings: Risk of tachyphylaxis (diminishing effect over time); cardiac side effects possible; short-term use preferred.

medications.name: Domperidone
medications.use: Effective prokinetic; reduces nausea and vomiting. Not FDA-approved in the US but used in many other countries.
medications.warnings: Cardiac QT prolongation risk; requires special access program in the US.

medications.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
medications.use: Relief of nausea; does not improve gastric emptying rate
medications.dosage: 4 or 8 mg up to 3 times daily

medications.name: Prochlorperazine
medications.use: Symptomatic relief of nausea and vomiting

medications.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
medications.use: Mild antiemetic; often used for nausea relief in gastroparesis

medications.name: Tricyclic Antidepressants (low-dose nortriptyline or amitriptyline)
medications.use: For nausea and abdominal pain not responding to prokinetics; modulates gut-brain communication
medications.warnings: Anticholinergic effects may further delay gastric emptying at higher doses.

nutritional_support.enteral_nutrition: Jejunostomy tube (J-tube) feeding used when oral intake is insufficient; bypasses the stomach.
nutritional_support.parenteral_nutrition: IV nutrition delivery directly into bloodstream; used in most severe cases when GI tract cannot be used.
nutritional_support.oral_supplements: Liquid nutritional supplements (Ensure, Boost) are often better tolerated than solid foods and provide necessary calories and protein.

gastritis_diet.healing_program_overview: The gastritis healing program focuses on three pillars: (1) Diet change, (2) Habit and lifestyle change, (3) Stress management. A 90-day healing period is recommended.
foods_to_eliminate: Acidic vegetables (tomatoes, tomato sauce, tomato paste)
Sugary and carbonated drinks (soda, energy drinks)
Processed and packaged foods (additives and preservatives worsen inflammation)

ingredient_substitutions.substitute: Almond milk, rice milk, oat milk (if tolerated)
Extra virgin olive oil, coconut oil (in moderation)

bad_habits_to_avoid: Skipping meals (prolongs stomach acid exposure to the lining)
Eating extremely hot or cold foods
Drinking while eating (dilutes stomach acid, disrupts digestion)
Overeating (prolongs food in stomach, increases acid irritation)
Stress eating or skipping meals due to stress
positive_habits: Chew food thoroughly (to mashed potato consistency)
Sit upright for at least 1 hour after eating
Stay hydrated throughout the day (sip, don't gulp)
Exercise moderately — walking improves gastric motility
Practice stress management (mindfulness, meditation, diaphragmatic breathing)
Plan meals in advance to avoid impulsive poor food choices
Cook in larger batches to have gastritis-friendly food ready
Maintain a food diary to identify personal triggers

gastroparesis_diet.overview: The goal is to reduce symptoms and maintain adequate nutrition. Liquids pass through the stomach more easily than solids. When symptoms are active, start with a liquid diet and advance to soft foods as tolerated.
gastroparesis_diet.meal_frequency: Eat 5–6 small meals per day. Each meal should be approximately 1 to 1.5 cups of food. Avoid large meals.
key_principles: Reduce fat intake — fat slows stomach emptying
Reduce fiber intake — high fiber can cause bezoar formation (a blockage in the stomach)
Chew all food to a mashed potato or pudding-like consistency
Drink beverages between meals, not during
Sit upright for 2–3 hours after eating
Avoid lying down or reclining after eating
Avoid carbonated beverages and chewing gum (cause air bubbles)
Exercise (walking after meals helps stomach emptying)
Keep blood sugar controlled if diabetic

grains.qualities: Less than 3g fiber per serving; white/refined flour; soft

protein.qualities: Lean (less than 5% fat); well-cooked; very tender; moist; finely chopped

vegetables.qualities: Less than 3g fiber per serving; well-cooked; canned; no skin

fruits.qualities: Less than 3g fiber per serving; well-cooked or canned; no skin
examples: Peach or pear cups in water (canned)

sample_meal_plan_1.breakfast: 1 slice white toast, 1 egg scrambled in 1 tsp canola oil, 1 cup peach nectar
sample_meal_plan_1.morning_snack: Smoothie: 1/2 banana, 1/2 cup low-fat Greek yogurt, 1 cup 2% milk
sample_meal_plan_1.lunch: 2 oz canned chicken mixed with 1 tsp mayonnaise, 9 saltine crackers, 1/2 cup applesauce
sample_meal_plan_1.afternoon_snack: 1 slice white toast with 1 tbsp smooth peanut butter
sample_meal_plan_1.dinner: 2 oz baked fish, 1/2 cup mashed potatoes, 3/4 cup green beans sautéed in 1 tsp olive oil

faq.question: What is the difference between gastritis and gastroparesis?
faq.answer: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining, caused by factors like H. pylori infection, NSAIDs, alcohol, or stress. Gastroparesis is a motility disorder where the stomach empties too slowly due to nerve damage, not inflammation. Both can cause nausea and discomfort, but they have different causes, diagnoses, and management strategies.

faq.question: What foods should I avoid with gastritis?
faq.answer: Avoid acidic foods (citrus, tomatoes), alcohol, coffee, carbonated drinks, spicy foods, fried/fatty foods, processed foods, excessive salt, and NSAIDs. Also avoid overeating and skipping meals. Refer to the gastritis_diet section for a detailed list.

faq.question: What foods should I avoid with gastroparesis?
faq.answer: Avoid high-fat foods, high-fiber foods, raw vegetables, tough meats, beans/lentils, most raw fruits, carbonated beverages, alcohol, and coffee. Fat and fiber both slow stomach emptying. Refer to the gastroparesis_diet section for a complete food list.

faq.question: Can I use probiotics for gastritis?
faq.answer: Yes, certain probiotic strains (especially Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species) have shown benefits for gastritis, particularly H. pylori-associated gastritis. They can help competitively exclude H. pylori, reduce inflammation, and support mucosal healing. Always consult your healthcare provider for strain-specific recommendations.

faq.question: What is H. pylori and how is it treated?
faq.answer: Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that infects the gastric mucosa and is the most aggressive cause of chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Standard treatment is triple therapy: two antibiotics (clarithromycin + amoxicillin) plus a proton pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole), taken for 10–14 days. Success rate is about 80%, decreasing due to antibiotic resistance. Natural anti-adhesion compounds (cranberry, licorice root, green tea catechins) may complement conventional treatment.

faq.question: How long does it take to heal gastritis?
faq.answer: This varies significantly by cause and severity. Acute gastritis from a specific trigger (e.g., stopping NSAIDs) may resolve in days to weeks. Chronic gastritis from H. pylori requires treatment of the infection. The Gastritis Healing Book recommends a 90-day foundational healing period combining diet change, lifestyle modification, and stress management. Always work with a healthcare provider.

faq.question: What is the Low FODMAP diet and who is it for?
faq.answer: The Low FODMAP diet is designed for people with IBS, gas, bloating, and bowel irritability. It eliminates fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs) that pull water into the small intestine and are fermented by gut bacteria, causing symptoms. It typically involves a strict elimination phase followed by gradual reintroduction to identify personal triggers. Symptom improvement may take up to 12 weeks.

faq.question: Can diet alone cure gastritis?
faq.answer: Diet is a crucial part of gastritis management but may not be sufficient alone. If H. pylori is present, antibiotic eradication therapy is necessary. NSAIDs should be stopped if possible. Diet changes reduce irritation, support mucosal healing, and decrease inflammation, but they work best alongside appropriate medical treatment and lifestyle changes.

faq.question: What natural remedies help with gastritis?
faq.answer: Evidence-supported options include: DGL licorice (increases mucus protection), Slippery Elm (mucilage coating), Aloe Vera juice (anti-inflammatory), L-Glutamine (stomach lining repair), Zinc Carnosine (healing, anti-inflammatory), probiotics (Lactobacillus strains), green tea catechins (anti-H. pylori), chamomile tea (soothing), and potato juice (natural antacid). Always consult a healthcare provider before starting supplements.

faq.question: I have gastroparesis and diabetes — what should I know?
faq.answer: Diabetes is the most common cause of gastroparesis. Gastroparesis makes blood sugar control very difficult because food absorption becomes unpredictable. You should monitor blood sugar more frequently, work with a diabetes educator and dietitian to adjust your insulin timing, and keep blood sugars in goal ranges — high blood sugar directly worsens stomach emptying. Focus on small, frequent low-fat, low-fiber meals.

faq.question: What beverages are safe with gastroparesis?
faq.answer: Safe options include clear broths, Pedialyte, gelatin, popsicles, sports drinks mixed with water, and water. Avoid coffee, soda and carbonated beverages, milkshakes, sweet tea, caffeinated teas, and alcohol. Smoothies made with low-fat, low-fiber ingredients are excellent for maintaining calories and nutrition.

faq.question: Is gluten-free diet needed for gastritis?
faq.answer: Not necessarily for everyone. The Gastritis Healing Book recommends eliminating gluten as part of an anti-inflammatory gastritis healing program, as it may irritate sensitive individuals. However, this is not a universal medical recommendation. If you have celiac disease or proven gluten sensitivity, a gluten-free diet is medically necessary. Discuss with your healthcare provider.

faq.question: What is the difference between gastritis and GERD?
faq.answer: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining itself, caused by H. pylori, NSAIDs, alcohol, or stress. GERD (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) is when stomach acid frequently flows back into the esophagus, causing heartburn and esophageal damage. They can co-exist — for example, low stomach acid from gastritis may contribute to GERD, and NSAID use can cause both.

faq.question: What is the difference between gastritis and a peptic ulcer?
faq.answer: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining; it may or may not cause visible tissue damage. A peptic ulcer is an open sore (erosion through the full mucosal layer) in the stomach or duodenum. Untreated gastritis, especially from H. pylori, can progress to peptic ulcer disease. Both share similar causes (H. pylori, NSAIDs).

faq.question: What is the updated H. pylori treatment in 2024?
faq.answer: The 2024 ACG (American College of Gastroenterology) guidelines now recommend Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (BQT) as the preferred first-line treatment — consisting of a PPI, bismuth, nitroimidazole, and tetracycline for 14 days. The older clarithromycin-based triple therapy is no longer recommended as first-line because resistance to clarithromycin exceeds 30% in many US regions. Alternative options include rifabutin triple therapy or vonoprazan dual therapy. Always follow your doctor's guidance based on your local resistance patterns.

faq.question: What medications are used for gastroparesis?
faq.answer: The only FDA-approved medication specifically for gastroparesis in the US is metoclopramide (Reglan) — a prokinetic drug that helps the stomach contract and empty faster. It should be used for no more than 12 weeks due to risk of tardive dyskinesia. Other options include low-dose erythromycin (for motility), antiemetics like ondansetron and prochlorperazine (for nausea relief), and domperidone (not FDA-approved in the US). For pain, non-narcotic medicines are preferred as opioids worsen gastroparesis.

faq.question: Is IBS dangerous? Does it cause cancer?
faq.answer: No, IBS (Irritable Bowel Syndrome) does NOT cause permanent damage to the intestines and does NOT increase the risk of colon cancer. It is a functional disorder — meaning the bowel works abnormally but is not structurally damaged. IBS is a chronic, manageable condition. However, certain symptoms like blood in stool, unintended weight loss, or symptoms starting after age 50 require medical evaluation to rule out more serious conditions.

faq.question: How do I know if I have H. pylori?
faq.answer: H. pylori can be detected through: (1) Urea breath test — drink a liquid containing urea; if H. pylori is present, it breaks it into carbon dioxide detectable in your breath; (2) Stool antigen test — detects H. pylori proteins in stool; (3) Blood antibody test — shows past or present infection; (4) Endoscopy with biopsy — the most definitive test, allows direct examination of stomach lining and tissue testing. Your doctor will choose the appropriate test based on your symptoms and situation.

faq.question: What are warning signs I need to go to emergency care for stomach problems?
faq.answer: Seek emergency care immediately if you have: black, tarry, or bloody stool (may indicate stomach or intestinal bleeding); vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds; sudden, severe abdominal pain (possible ulcer perforation — a medical emergency); signs of severe dehydration (dizziness, no urination, rapid heartbeat). These are potentially life-threatening and require immediate medical attention.

faq.question: Can children get gastritis?
faq.answer: Yes, children can develop gastritis. H. pylori infection can occur in childhood, and H. pylori bacteria may spread through contact with an infected person's vomit, stool, or saliva. NSAIDs and certain infections can also cause gastritis in children. Symptoms in children may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and poor appetite. A pediatric gastroenterologist should be consulted for proper diagnosis and treatment.

faq.question: Can I exercise with gastritis or gastroparesis?
faq.answer: Yes — moderate exercise is generally beneficial. For gastritis, exercise helps manage stress (a major gastritis trigger) and supports overall digestive health. For gastroparesis, walking after meals is specifically recommended as it has been shown to improve stomach emptying in healthy individuals. Avoid vigorous exercise immediately after eating. High-impact exercises that compress the abdomen may worsen symptoms. Always follow your healthcare provider's guidance.

faq.question: What is Gastric Electrical Stimulation (GES) for gastroparesis?
faq.answer: Gastric Electrical Stimulation (GES) is a device surgically implanted in the abdomen that sends mild electrical pulses to the stomach muscles to help control nausea and vomiting in gastroparesis. It is used only for gastroparesis caused by diabetes or unknown causes (idiopathic), and only when medications fail to control symptoms. It is approved by the FDA under a humanitarian device exemption. GES improves symptoms in many patients but does not consistently improve gastric emptying rates.

stress_and_lifestyle.stress_impact: Chronic stress reduces protective gastric factors, increases stomach acid production, and influences unhealthy coping behaviors (alcohol, smoking, poor diet). The gut-brain relationship is well established — psychological well-being directly affects digestive health.

gastritis_in_brief.key_treatment: Antibiotics (for H. pylori) + PPIs; dietary modification; avoid NSAIDs/alcohol
gastritis_in_brief.when_to_see_doctor: Persistent pain, nausea, bloody stool, vomiting blood

gastroparesis_in_brief.what: Stomach takes too long to empty (delayed gastric emptying); nerves to stomach damaged
gastroparesis_in_brief.key_treatment: Small frequent low-fat low-fiber meals; metoclopramide (FDA-approved); blood sugar control in diabetes
gastroparesis_in_brief.when_to_see_doctor: Persistent nausea/vomiting, weight loss, inability to eat, blood sugar problems

IBS_in_brief.what: Disorder of gut-brain interaction causing abdominal pain with altered bowel habits
IBS_in_brief.most_common_cause: Gut-brain axis dysfunction; food triggers (FODMAPs); stress; microbiome changes
IBS_in_brief.key_treatment: Low FODMAP diet; stress management; fiber; antispasmodics; CBT
IBS_in_brief.does_not_cause: Tissue damage, cancer, or permanent intestinal injury

GERD_in_brief.what: Chronic acid reflux causing heartburn and esophageal damage
GERD_in_brief.most_common_cause: Weakened lower esophageal sphincter; obesity; certain foods
GERD_in_brief.key_treatment: Lifestyle changes; PPIs or H2 blockers; avoid trigger foods
GERD_in_brief.serious_complication: Barrett's esophagus (pre-cancerous); get regular monitoring if diagnosed
